etymology: From Pentecost, the feast fifty days after Passover (Greek pentekoste, fiftieth), on which the Spirit was poured out (Acts 2); the movement names itself for that day.
biblical_def: Pentecostalism is the early-twentieth-century movement, dated commonly to the Azusa Street revival of 1906, that teaches a "second blessing" of Spirit-baptism subsequent to conversion, evidenced by speaking in tongues, and that the sign-gifts of the apostolic age — tongues, healing, prophecy — continue undiminished today. From it grew the prosperity offshoots that promise health and wealth to the faithful. This dictionary honors the hunger for God that animated many early adherents and the missionary zeal that carried the name of Christ across the earth. Yet it names the movement's governing premise a departure from Scripture rightly read. The sign-gifts attended the laying of the foundation, "the apostles and prophets" (Eph 2:20), and authenticated the Word as it was given; they were never promised as the perpetual possession of the church. The canon is closed; God speaks now in the Son and in the completed Scriptures, "that the man of God may be perfect" (2 Tim 3:17). Spirit-baptism is not a second experience for the elite but the one washing by which all believers are made one body (1 Cor 12:13). This dictionary confesses the cessationist position of the Reformed confessions: the extraordinary gifts have ceased, and the prosperity gospel is no gospel at all, but a covetous counterfeit.
webster_summary: A modern movement, arising about 1906, holding that Spirit-baptism is a second work evidenced by tongues and that the miraculous gifts continue. The Reformed churches judge this a departure from the closed canon.
webster_full: PENTECOSTALISM, noun. A religious movement of the twentieth century teaching a second baptism of the Spirit, tongues as its sign, and the continuance of the sign-gifts.
Distinguished from the apostolic Pentecost of Acts, which was once and unrepeatable.
"Are all apostles? are all prophets? are all teachers? are all workers of miracles?" (1 Cor 12:29).
Holds that what God gave to found His church He gives still to every age; this the cessationist denies.
Its prosperity offshoots, promising wealth to the believing, are condemned as covetousness mistaken for godliness.
scriptures: Acts 2:4
And they were all filled with the Holy Ghost, and began to speak with other tongues, as the Spirit gave them utterance.
Charity never faileth: but whether there be prophecies, they shall fail; whether there be tongues, they shall cease; whether there be knowledge, it shall vanish away.
Eph 2:20
And are built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner stone;
1 Tim 6:5
Perverse disputings of men of corrupt minds, and destitute of the truth, supposing that gain is godliness: from such withdraw thyself.
corruption_summary: Pentecostalism makes the foundation-laying gifts perpetual and Spirit-baptism a second experience, against a closed canon; its prosperity offshoots equate gain with godliness.
corruption_paragraphs: The continuationist claim treats the extraordinary gifts of the apostolic age as the abiding norm. But Scripture binds those gifts to the laying of the foundation. Tongues were a sign "to them that believe not" (1 Cor 14:22), a judgment-token to unbelieving Israel; healing and prophecy authenticated the apostles as bearers of new revelation. When the foundation was laid and the canon closed, the signs that attended its laying ceased, as Paul foretold they would (1 Cor 13:8-10). To demand them now is to reopen what God has shut, and to treat the perfect Scriptures as insufficient.

Worse is the prosperity offshoot, which teaches that faith is a force compelling God to grant health and riches. This is the very error Paul names: men "supposing that gain is godliness" (1 Tim 6:5). It preaches a cross-less Christ and a self-serving faith, and it preys on the poor it claims to enrich. Against both the milder continuationism and its grasping offspring, this dictionary confesses that God now speaks in His Son by the finished Word, and that the Spirit's great gift is not tongues or treasure but a new heart.
roots_summary: The name derives from the apostolic Pentecost of Acts 2, which the movement wrongly treats as a repeatable pattern rather than a once-for-all founding event.
roots_lines: Greek pentekoste, fiftieth, the feast fifty days after Passover.
Acts 2 records the Spirit poured out to launch the church's mission.
That outpouring was foundational and unrepeatable, not a template for a "second blessing."
The movement borrows the name to claim continuity with that founding event.
Scripture, rightly read, ties tongues and signs to the apostolic foundation now laid.
usage: Pentecostalism spread with remarkable speed across the globe in the twentieth century.
The cessationist parts ways with Pentecostalism precisely over the closed canon.
The prosperity branch of Pentecostalism turns faith into a tool for gain.

etymology: From Greek charisma, a gift of grace (plural charismata), the term Paul uses for the Spirit's gifts (1 Cor 12); renewal from Latin renovare, to make new again.
biblical_def: The Charismatic Renewal is the mid-twentieth-century movement that carried Pentecostal practice — tongues, prophecy, healing — out of the Pentecostal denominations and into mainline Protestant and Roman Catholic churches, beginning in the 1960s. From it later grew the New Apostolic Reformation, the International House of Prayer (IHOP), and the ministries gathered around Bethel Church, with their claim to restored offices of apostle and prophet and their continuous "words from the Lord." This dictionary acknowledges that many caught up in the Renewal sought a deeper devotion than the dead formalism around them, and that desire is not to be despised. Yet the movement's defining claim — that modern apostles and prophets speak fresh revelation today — strikes at the closed canon. The apostles were eyewitnesses of the risen Christ, appointed to lay the foundation once (Eph 2:20; Acts 1:21-22); their office cannot be reconstituted. To "prophesy" alongside Scripture is to add to the Word that God has finished, against the warning "Add thou not unto his words" (Prov 30:6). This dictionary confesses cessationism: God's public revelation is complete in the sixty-six books, and no man may claim apostolic authority or fresh prophetic oracles in this age.
webster_summary: A movement from the 1960s carrying Pentecostal practice into mainline and Roman Catholic churches, later producing the New Apostolic Reformation, IHOP, and Bethel. Its claim of modern apostles and prophets corrupts the closed canon.
webster_full: CHARISMATIC RENEWAL, noun. A twentieth-century movement importing tongues, prophecy, and healing into established Protestant and Roman communions.
Its later forms claim to restore the offices of apostle and prophet.
"Add thou not unto his words, lest he reprove thee, and thou be found a liar" (Prov 30:6).
The apostolic office was founded on eyewitness of the risen Christ and cannot be repeated.
Where new oracles are claimed, the sufficiency of the closed canon is denied.
scriptures: Eph 2:20
And are built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner stone;
Prov 30:6
Add thou not unto his words, lest he reprove thee, and thou be found a liar.
Acts 1:22
Beginning from the baptism of John, unto that same day that he was taken up from us, must one be ordained to be a witness with us of his resurrection.
Heb 1:1
God, who at sundry times and in divers manners spake in time past unto the fathers by the prophets,
corruption_summary: The Renewal and its New Apostolic offshoots claim living apostles and prophets bearing fresh revelation, adding to the finished Word and denying the closed canon.
corruption_paragraphs: The gravest error is the claim to a restored apostolate. An apostle, in the New Testament sense, was an eyewitness of the resurrection commissioned directly by Christ to lay the church's foundation (Acts 1:21-22; Eph 2:20). That foundation is laid once. When modern movements ordain "apostles" and receive ongoing "prophetic words," they treat the canon as still open and the Scriptures as a beginning rather than a completed deposit. The warning stands: "Add thou not unto his words" (Prov 30:6).

The Renewal's spread into Roman Catholicism compounded the confusion, for it grafted experiential gifts onto a system that already denies sola fide and exalts a treasury of merit. The later excesses — IHOP's ceaseless "prophetic" output, Bethel's signs-and-wonders culture, the New Apostolic Reformation's governmental apostles — are sober concerns, not mere differences of style. This dictionary honors the longing for the living God that drew many in, while confessing that He is found not in fresh oracles but in His finished Word, "in these last days spoken unto us by his Son" (Heb 1:2).
roots_summary: The name comes from charismata, Paul's word for the Spirit's gifts, which the movement claims to recover in full apostolic measure.
roots_lines: Greek charisma, a grace-gift; plural charismata in 1 Cor 12.
Renewal signals a claimed revival of those gifts in the wider church.
The movement reads 1 Corinthians 12-14 as binding on every age alike.
Cessationists read the same chapters as describing the apostolic foundation now laid.
Where apostles and prophets are claimed anew, the closed canon is at stake.
usage: The Charismatic Renewal swept into mainline parishes that had grown cold and formal.
Critics of the Charismatic Renewal point first to its claim of living apostles.
The New Apostolic Reformation is the most far-reaching offshoot of the Charismatic Renewal.

etymology: Gospel from Old English gōdspel, good tidings; coalition from Latin coalescere, to grow together — a banding together around the gospel.
biblical_def: The Gospel Coalition is a contemporary network of Reformed-leaning evangelicals founded in 2005 under the leadership of Timothy Keller and D. A. Carson, gathering pastors and writers around a shared confessional statement and a "gospel-centered" vision of ministry. This dictionary honors much in it: its written confession affirms the Trinity, the authority and inerrancy of Scripture, justification by faith alone, penal substitution, and salvation by grace; its theological vision presses for Christ-centered preaching that reads the whole Bible as pointing to the Redeemer (Luke 24:27); and its catechetical and reading resources have served many in the recovery of doctrine. It has labored to keep the gospel central where evangelicalism drifted toward moralism on one side and license on the other. Soberly, this dictionary notes the strains native to any broad-tent coalition: a confession framed to admit both Baptist and paedobaptist, both complementarian and the soft edges of the same, will at points speak less plainly than a full confession like the 1689, and a broad tent invites the pressures of the surrounding culture. These are concerns to weigh, not grievances to manufacture. This dictionary commends the Coalition's gospel-centered confession while measuring it, as all things, by the standard of the written Word.
webster_summary: A network of Reformed evangelicals founded in 2005 by Keller and Carson, centered on a gospel confession and Christ-centered preaching. Its confession is sound; the breadth of its coalition warrants sober watchfulness.
webster_full: THE GOSPEL COALITION, noun. A contemporary evangelical network organized around a shared confession of the gospel and Reformed soteriology.
Founded 2005 under Timothy Keller and D. A. Carson.
"And beginning at Moses and all the prophets, he expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself" (Luke 24:27).
Affirms inerrancy, justification by faith alone, and penal substitution.
A broad coalition; its breadth is both its reach and the ground of sober watchfulness.
scriptures: Luke 24:27
And beginning at Moses and all the prophets, he expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself.
For I delivered unto you first of all that which I also received, how that Christ died for our sins according to the scriptures;
Gal 1:8
But though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed.
Jude 1:3

Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints.
corruption_summary: The Gospel Coalition faces no postmodern redefinition; the watchfulness it warrants is the ordinary care owed to any broad-tent confession in a drifting culture.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The Coalition is a living evangelical body, not a contested term; the principle to recover is therefore measured discernment. Scripture commands that we "earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints" (Jude 3) and that we "prove all things; hold fast that which is good" (1 Thess 5:21). A confession framed to gather Baptists and paedobaptists under one roof will speak more generally than the 1689 on the sacraments and the church, and a wide platform is more exposed to the pressures of the age than a narrow pulpit.

Honesty requires naming both the good and the caution without overstatement. The good is real: a clear written gospel, Christ-centered exposition, sound men recovering Reformed truth for a new generation. The caution is ordinary: breadth dilutes precision, and broad coalitions must guard against cultural drift on the questions a generous statement leaves open. This dictionary commends the genuine service and confesses that every network, however sound its founding charter, stands or falls by the same Word it claims to honor — "to the law and to the testimony" (Isa 8:20).
roots_summary: The name joins gospel, the good tidings of Christ crucified, to coalition, a growing-together of churches around that message.
roots_lines: Gospel, Old English gōdspel, good news, rendering Greek euangelion.
Coalition, Latin coalescere, to grow together into one.
The name claims the gospel itself as the uniting center.
Its founding confession sets the boundaries of that union.
The breadth of the coalition is the chief object of sober watchfulness.
usage: The Gospel Coalition publishes articles, reviews, and reading plans for a wide readership.
Many young Reformed pastors first encountered Christ-centered preaching through the Gospel Coalition.
A confessional Baptist reads the Gospel Coalition with appreciation and measured discernment.

etymology: From the nine "marks" of a healthy church set out by Mark Dever; mark from Old English mearc, a sign or boundary, as in the historic notae ecclesiae, the marks of the true church.
biblical_def: 9Marks is the ministry founded by Mark Dever, pastor of Capitol Hill Baptist Church, devoted to recovering the marks of a healthy local church. The nine are: expository preaching; biblical theology; a biblical understanding of the gospel; a biblical understanding of conversion; biblical evangelism; biblical church membership; biblical church discipline; biblical discipleship and growth; and biblical church leadership. This dictionary commends the ministry without reservation on these heads. Each mark is a recovery of plain New Testament order: that the Word be preached by opening the text and pressing its point (Neh 8:8; 2 Tim 4:2); that the gospel of substitution and the new birth not be assumed but stated; that membership be a meaningful covenant of accountable believers, not a roll of names; that discipline, neglected for a century, be restored as Christ commanded (Matt 18:15-17); and that the church be led by a plurality of qualified elders. These are not innovations but the regulative principle applied to congregational life. This dictionary confesses with 9Marks that the local church, rightly ordered under the Word, is the ordinary means by which Christ keeps and grows His people, and gladly commends a ministry that has called many congregations back to that order.
webster_summary: Mark Dever's ministry recovering nine marks of a healthy church, from expository preaching to elder leadership. This dictionary commends it as a faithful application of New Testament church order.
webster_full: 9MARKS, noun. A ministry recovering the marks of a healthy local church: preaching, gospel, conversion, evangelism, membership, discipline, discipleship, and leadership.
Founded by Mark Dever of Capitol Hill Baptist Church.
"So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading" (Neh 8:8).
Restores church discipline and meaningful membership long neglected.
Commended as the regulative principle applied to the ordering of the congregation.
scriptures: 2 Tim 4:2
Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine.
Neh 8:8
So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading.
Matt 18:17
And if he shall neglect to hear them, tell it unto the church: but if he neglect to hear the church, let him be unto thee as an heathen man and a publican.
Titus 1:5
For this cause left I thee in Crete, that thou shouldest set in order the things that are wanting, and ordain elders in every city, as I had appointed thee:
corruption_summary: 9Marks faces no postmodern redefinition; the principle to recover is the ordinary New Testament order of a healthy church that the ministry exists to restore.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. 9Marks is a contemporary ministry, not a contested term, and the principle to recover is the very burden of its work: the health of the local church. For a century much of evangelicalism let membership become nominal, discipline lapse entirely, and preaching drift from the text to the topical. 9Marks calls the church back to "Preach the word" (2 Tim 4:2), to meaningful membership, and to the discipline Christ Himself appointed (Matt 18:15-17).

The nine marks are not a clever program but a summary of plain apostolic instruction. Expository preaching honors the sufficiency of Scripture; biblical conversion guards against false assurance; church discipline guards the purity of Christ's body; plurality of elders follows Paul's charge to Titus (Titus 1:5). This dictionary commends the ministry as a recovery, not an invention, and confesses with it that the ordinary means of grace, ministered in a rightly ordered church, are how the Shepherd keeps His sheep.
roots_summary: The name echoes the historic notae ecclesiae, the marks of the true church, applied here to nine features of congregational health.
roots_lines: Mark, Old English mearc, a sign, boundary, or token.
The Reformers spoke of the notae ecclesiae, marks of the true church.
9Marks names nine concrete features of a healthy congregation.
Each is drawn from plain New Testament instruction, not novelty.
The marks together apply the regulative principle to church life.
usage: Many pastors restructured their membership process after reading the 9Marks books.
9Marks has done more than any ministry to recover church discipline in our day.
The nine marks of 9Marks are simply New Testament church order stated plainly.

etymology: Temperance from Latin temperare, to moderate or restrain; the historic name for self-control, one of the fruits of the Spirit (Gal 5:23).
biblical_def: The Temperance Movement was the nineteenth- and early-twentieth-century Christian effort against the ruin wrought by drunkenness, gathering churches, societies, and eventually political force against the saloon. This dictionary honors the biblical sobriety it defended. Scripture is plain that drunkenness is sin and folly: "Wine is a mocker, strong drink is raging: and whosoever is deceived thereby is not wise" (Prov 20:1); it paints the drunkard's misery in unsparing colors (Prov 23:29-35); and it commands, "be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess; but be filled with the Spirit" (Eph 5:18). The movement rightly saw families destroyed and consciences debauched by strong drink, and it labored to defend the weak. Yet this dictionary notes soberly where the movement overreached. Many of its leaders bound the conscience to total abstinence as a mark of holiness, going beyond what Scripture requires. But the Lord Himself made wine at Cana (John 2), Paul counseled Timothy to "use a little wine for thy stomach's sake" (1 Tim 5:23), and the Psalmist blesses God for "wine that maketh glad the heart of man" (Psa 104:15). The command is against drunkenness, not against the cup. This dictionary confesses biblical temperance — sober self-government under the Spirit — while refusing to add a law God did not give.
webster_summary: A Christian movement against drunkenness, peaking in the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. This dictionary honors the sobriety it defended while noting its overreach into binding total abstinence beyond Scripture.
webster_full: TEMPERANCE MOVEMENT, noun. A Christian campaign against drunkenness and the saloon, peaking from the early 1800s to Prohibition.
Rooted in the biblical condemnation of drunkenness as sin.
"Wine is a mocker, strong drink is raging: and whosoever is deceived thereby is not wise" (Prov 20:1).
Rightly forbade drunkenness; many leaders wrongly bound the conscience to total abstinence.
Scripture forbids being drunk with wine, not the moderate and thankful use of it.
scriptures: Prov 20:1
Wine is a mocker, strong drink is raging: and whosoever is deceived thereby is not wise.
Eph 5:18
And be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess; but be filled with the Spirit;
Prov 23:31
Look not thou upon the wine when it is red, when it giveth his colour in the cup, when it moveth itself aright.
Drink no longer water, but use a little wine for thy stomach's sake and thine often infirmities.
corruption_summary: The Temperance Movement's overreach was to bind the conscience to total abstinence as a mark of holiness, adding a requirement Scripture does not impose.
corruption_paragraphs: The movement's strength was its faithful witness against a real and devastating sin. Drunkenness wrecks the body, beggars the family, and inflames every other vice; Scripture warns of it again and again (Prov 23:29-35; 1 Cor 6:10; Gal 5:21). In defending sobriety and protecting the vulnerable, the temperance churches did genuine good, and this dictionary honors them for it.

Its overreach was to mistake total abstinence for holiness and to press it upon every conscience. But Christ turned water into wine at Cana (John 2:1-11), Paul prescribed wine to Timothy (1 Tim 5:23), and the Psalmist names wine among God's good gifts (Psa 104:15). To forbid what God permits is to add to His law, the error of the Pharisee, "teaching for doctrines the commandments of men" (Matt 15:9). This dictionary confesses biblical temperance — Spirit-wrought self-control that abhors drunkenness — while leaving the cup itself to Christian liberty and a charitable conscience.
roots_summary: Temperance renders the biblical virtue of self-control, a fruit of the Spirit, which the movement defended even as some pressed it past Scripture's bounds.
roots_lines: Latin temperare, to moderate, restrain, or govern.
The KJV renders the virtue "temperance" in Gal 5:23 and 2 Pet 1:6.
It denotes Spirit-wrought self-government, not necessarily total abstinence.
The movement took the name for its campaign against drunkenness.
Where it bound abstinence as a law, it strained beyond the word.
usage: The Temperance Movement drew much of its strength from the revival churches.
A defender of biblical temperance condemns drunkenness without forbidding the cup.
The Temperance Movement's political arm pressed at last for national Prohibition.

etymology: From Zoroaster (Greek for the Persian Zarathustra), its founding teacher; the religion of ancient Persia centered on the god Ahura Mazda.
biblical_def: Zoroastrianism is the ancient Persian religion of Zoroaster, teaching a cosmic dualism between Ahura Mazda, the good god of light, and Angra Mainyu (Ahriman), the principle of evil and darkness, locked in struggle until a final consummation. This dictionary records the religion as a historical fact and a pagan error. Its chief modern interest lies in a claim of the critical academy: that Israel borrowed its monotheism, its angels and demons, and its doctrines of resurrection, judgment, and the age to come from Persia during the Babylonian exile. This dictionary rejects that claim outright. The God of Israel revealed Himself as the one true God from the beginning — to Abraham long before any Persian empire, declaring "I am the Almighty God" (Gen 17:1) — and the Shema, "the LORD our God is one LORD" (Deut 6:4), was given through Moses centuries before the exile. The dualism of Zoroaster, with two competing principles, is the opposite of biblical monotheism, in which God alone is sovereign and even the powers of darkness are His creatures, wholly subject to Him: "I form the light, and create darkness" (Isa 45:7). Israel's faith is not a late synthesis assembled from pagan neighbors but original revelation, earlier and given by God. This dictionary confesses that Scripture's truth descends from heaven, not from Persia.
webster_summary: The ancient Persian dualism of Ahura Mazda and Angra Mainyu. This dictionary rebuts the academic claim that Israel borrowed its monotheism and eschatology from it during the exile.
webster_full: ZOROASTRIANISM, noun. The ancient Persian religion teaching a cosmic struggle between a good god and an evil principle.
Named for its teacher Zoroaster (Zarathustra).
"I form the light, and create darkness: I make peace, and create evil: I the LORD do all these things" (Isa 45:7).
Its dualism stands opposed to the one sovereign God of Scripture.
The claim that Israel borrowed its faith from Persia is rejected as false.
scriptures: Deut 6:4
Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God is one LORD:
Isa 45:7
I form the light, and create darkness: I make peace, and create evil: I the LORD do all these things.
Gen 17:1
And when Abram was ninety years old and nine, the LORD appeared to Abram, and said unto him, I am the Almighty God; walk before me, and be thou perfect.
Isa 45:5
I am the LORD, and there is none else, there is no God beside me: I girded thee, though thou hast not known me:
corruption_summary: The corruption is the academic claim that Israel borrowed its monotheism, angelology, and eschatology from Persian Zoroastrianism during the exile — a theory that denies the originality and divine origin of Scripture.
corruption_paragraphs: The critical theory holds that Israel's mature doctrines of one God, of angels and demons, of resurrection and final judgment, were late developments absorbed from Persia after the exile — in short, that the Bible's revelation is a borrowed and assembled thing. This rests on the late-composition assumptions of the historical-critical method, which this dictionary rejects as a denial of inspiration. The monotheism it calls late was confessed by Abraham (Gen 17:1) and codified through Moses (Deut 6:4) centuries before Cyrus reigned.

The biblical and Zoroastrian schemes are not parent and child but opposites. Zoroaster posits two principles, good and evil, each in some sense original. Scripture knows one God who creates all, including the darkness and the powers of evil, which remain His subjects: "I form the light, and create darkness" (Isa 45:7). Where Persia has a struggle between near-equals, the Bible has absolute sovereignty. Surface resemblances, where they exist, prove nothing but that fallen men retain broken fragments of truth; the fullness was given by revelation to Israel and stands earlier, not later. This dictionary confesses Scripture as the original and inspired Word, not a salvage of pagan myth.
roots_summary: The name derives from the prophet Zoroaster; its dualism of light and darkness stands opposed to the Bible's confession of one sovereign Creator of both.
roots_lines: Zoroaster, the Greek form of the Persian Zarathustra.
Centered on Ahura Mazda, the "wise lord" of light.
Opposed by Angra Mainyu (Ahriman), the destructive spirit.
Its cosmic dualism contradicts biblical monotheism.
Scripture answers it: the LORD alone forms both light and darkness (Isa 45:7).
usage: Zoroastrianism was the imperial religion of Persia when Daniel served in Babylon.
Skeptics appeal to Zoroastrianism to explain away the originality of Israel's faith.
The dualism of Zoroastrianism cannot be reconciled with the one God of Scripture.

etymology: Hebrew from the language of the patriarchs and prophets; Bible from Greek biblia, books — here the modern academy's preferred label for what Christians call the Old Testament.
biblical_def: "Hebrew Bible" is the modern academy's preferred name for the books Christians have always called the Old Testament. It is favored in the university because it appears neutral: it avoids the Christian category "Old," which implies a "New" and a fulfillment in Christ, and it satisfies a setting that wishes to study these books apart from the church's confession. This dictionary explains the term in order to decline it. The label is not innocent; it embodies a judgment — that the Hebrew Scriptures stand on their own, complete in themselves, owned by no covenant community in particular. But the Lord Jesus did not read them so. On the Emmaus road, "beginning at Moses and all the prophets, he expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself" (Luke 24:27). He declared, "they are they which testify of me" (John 5:39). The apostles preached Christ from these very books (Acts 17:2-3). To call them merely the "Hebrew Bible" is to sever them from the One they were written to reveal. This dictionary therefore keeps "Old Testament" — old not as outdated but as the first and foundational covenant fulfilled in the new. The Hebrew Scriptures are Christian Scripture, read rightly only in Christ.
webster_summary: The academy's preferred label for the Old Testament, framed to avoid the Christian category. This dictionary keeps "Old Testament," for the Hebrew Scriptures are Christian Scripture fulfilled in Christ.
webster_full: HEBREW BIBLE, noun. The modern academic label for the Old Testament, chosen to appear neutral toward Christian and Jewish readings alike.
It avoids the term "Old," which implies fulfillment in a "New" Testament.
"Search the scriptures... they are they which testify of me" (John 5:39).
The label severs the books from the Christ they were written to reveal.
This dictionary keeps "Old Testament," for these are Christian Scripture in Christ.
scriptures: Luke 24:27
And beginning at Moses and all the prophets, he expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself.
John 5:39
Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life: and they are they which testify of me.
And that from a child thou hast known the holy scriptures, which are able to make thee wise unto salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus.
Luke 24:44

And he said unto them, These are the words which I spake unto you, while I was yet with you, that all things must be fulfilled, which were written in the law of Moses, and in the prophets, and in the psalms, concerning me.
corruption_summary: The corruption is the academic preference for "Hebrew Bible" over "Old Testament," a label that detaches the Hebrew Scriptures from their fulfillment in Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: The term is promoted as scholarly neutrality, but neutrality toward Christ is impossible; to set Him aside is already to take a side. By replacing "Old Testament" with "Hebrew Bible," the academy treats these books as a self-standing artifact of ancient religion rather than as the first volume of the one Christian Scripture. This fits the historical-critical posture, which reads the texts as the late and layered product of Israel's religious development rather than as the inspired and Christ-bearing Word.

The Lord answers the question Himself. He read Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms as concerning Him (Luke 24:44), and rebuked those who searched the Scriptures yet missed their testimony to Him (John 5:39). Paul reasoned with the Jews "out of the scriptures" that Jesus is the Christ (Acts 17:2-3). "Old Testament" confesses this: old as first and foundational, fulfilled and not annulled in the new. This dictionary keeps the historic name and confesses the Hebrew Scriptures to be Christian Scripture, "able to make thee wise unto salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus" (2 Tim 3:15).
roots_summary: The label joins Hebrew to Bible to name the Old Testament without its Christian frame; this dictionary reads those same books as fulfilled in Christ.
roots_lines: Hebrew, the language of Moses, the prophets, and the psalms.
Bible, from Greek biblia, the books.
The academy joins them to avoid the Christian word "Old."
"Old Testament" confesses fulfillment in a "New."
Christ read these books as testifying of Himself (Luke 24:27).
usage: University catalogs list the course as "Introduction to the Hebrew Bible."
The term "Hebrew Bible" quietly brackets the question of Christ.
This dictionary keeps "Old Testament" where the academy prefers "Hebrew Bible."

etymology: From lukewarm, Middle English lewk (tepid) + warm; the condition Christ names in the church of Laodicea, "neither cold nor hot" (Rev 3:15).
biblical_def: Lukewarmness is the spiritual condition of the church at Laodicea, which the risen Christ rebukes in the last of the seven letters: "I would thou wert cold or hot. So then because thou art lukewarm, and neither cold nor hot, I will spue thee out of my mouth" (Rev 3:15-16). It is the temper of self-sufficient complacency. Laodicea was rich, a banking and clothing city famed for a medicinal eye-salve, and the church had taken on the spirit of the town: "I am rich, and increased with goods, and have need of nothing" (Rev 3:17). Christ exposes the deadly self-deception — that they were in truth "wretched, and miserable, and poor, and blind, and naked." To such He gives counsel sharpened to their own trades: "buy of me gold tried in the fire, that thou mayest be rich; and white raiment, that thou mayest be clothed... and anoint thine eyes with eyesalve, that thou mayest see" (Rev 3:18). Yet even this letter of severest warning carries the tenderest call: "Behold, I stand at the door, and knock" (Rev 3:20). The remedy is to "be zealous therefore, and repent" (Rev 3:19). This dictionary confesses that lukewarmness is no harmless middle state but a thing Christ loathes, and that the only cure is the zeal of true repentance and renewed dependence on Him.
webster_summary: The complacent, self-sufficient state of the Laodicean church, "neither cold nor hot," which Christ threatens to spue out of His mouth. The remedy is to buy gold tried in the fire and to be zealous and repent.
webster_full: LUKEWARMNESS, noun. The tepid, self-satisfied spiritual state of the church at Laodicea, neither cold nor hot.
Marked by the boast "I am rich... and have need of nothing," while truly poor and blind.
"So then because thou art lukewarm, and neither cold nor hot, I will spue thee out of my mouth" (Rev 3:16).
Christ counsels the lukewarm to buy of Him gold tried in the fire and eyesalve to see.
The remedy: "be zealous therefore, and repent" (Rev 3:19).
scriptures: Rev 3:15
I know thy works, that thou art neither cold nor hot: I would thou wert cold or hot.
Rev 3:16
So then because thou art lukewarm, and neither cold nor hot, I will spue thee out of my mouth.
Rev 3:17
Because thou sayest, I am rich, and increased with goods, and have need of nothing; and knowest not that thou art wretched, and miserable, and poor, and blind, and naked:
Rev 3:19
As many as I love, I rebuke and chasten: be zealous therefore, and repent.
corruption_summary: Lukewarmness faces no postmodern redefinition; the principle to recover is the searching Laodicean warning against complacency masking spiritual poverty.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The danger Christ names at Laodicea is perennial and pressing, perhaps nowhere more than in a comfortable and prosperous age. The lukewarm church is not the persecuted church nor the heretical one; it is the satisfied one, sure of its wealth and unaware of its want. The deadliness lies precisely in the self-deception: "thou knowest not that thou art wretched" (Rev 3:17).

The positive principle to recover is the costly grace Christ offers in answer: gold tried in the fire, white raiment, and eyesalve — true righteousness, true covering, and true sight, all bought of Him and from no other store. The remedy is not redoubled self-effort but renewed dependence, "be zealous therefore, and repent" (Rev 3:19), opening the door to the Christ who knocks (Rev 3:20). This dictionary confesses that the chastening which exposes our poverty is a token of His love, and that the cure for the tepid heart is to come empty to Christ and be made rich in Him.
roots_summary: The word renders the Laodicean condition of tepid water — neither the cold of a refreshing spring nor the heat of a healing bath — fit only to be spued out.
roots_lines: Lukewarm, Middle English lewk, tepid, joined to warm.
Laodicea's water arrived tepid by aqueduct, sickening to drink.
Christ likens the church's state to that nauseating tepidity.
Neither the cold of a spring nor the heat of a bath profits.
The remedy is the zeal and repentance of Revelation 3:19.
usage: Lukewarmness is the besetting peril of a prosperous and untroubled church.
Christ deals more sharply with lukewarmness than with open opposition.
The cure for lukewarmness is to buy of Christ the gold tried in the fire.

etymology: From the charge to the church at Ephesus, "thou hast left thy first love" (Rev 2:4); first denoting the earliest and warmest devotion of the new convert.
biblical_def: "First love" is the phrase Christ uses in His letter to the church at Ephesus: "Nevertheless I have somewhat against thee, because thou hast left thy first love" (Rev 2:4). The Ephesian church was, by every outward measure, exemplary. Christ commends its works, its labor, its patience, its hatred of evil men, its testing and exposing of false apostles, its endurance for His name's sake without fainting (Rev 2:2-3). It was sound in doctrine and tireless in labor. Yet the searching eye of the Lord found a fatal cooling beneath the diligence: the ardent love that marked its beginning had grown cold. Orthodoxy and industry had outlasted affection. This is a sobering word, that a church may contend rightly for the truth and toil without ceasing, and still grieve its Lord by losing the first warmth of love to Him. The remedy Christ gives is threefold and exact: "Remember therefore from whence thou art fallen, and repent, and do the first works" (Rev 2:5) — remember the height from which the heart has slipped, repent of the cooling, and return to the deeds love first prompted. The warning is grave: else "I will remove thy candlestick out of his place." This dictionary confesses that sound doctrine and busy hands cannot substitute for love to Christ, and that the cooled heart is recovered by remembrance, repentance, and a return to first works.
webster_summary: The warm devotion of the Ephesian church which it had left, though sound in doctrine and labor (Rev 2:4). The threefold remedy: remember, repent, and do the first works.
webster_full: FIRST LOVE, noun. The earliest, ardent devotion to Christ which the Ephesian church had abandoned while remaining busy and orthodox.
Christ commended its labor and patience yet charged it with cooled affection.
"Nevertheless I have somewhat against thee, because thou hast left thy first love" (Rev 2:4).
Sound doctrine and tireless works cannot replace love to Christ.
The remedy: "remember... and repent, and do the first works" (Rev 2:5).
scriptures: Rev 2:4
Nevertheless I have somewhat against thee, because thou hast left thy first love.
Rev 2:5
Remember therefore from whence thou art fallen, and repent, and do the first works; or else I will come unto thee quickly, and will remove thy candlestick out of his place, except thou repent.
Rev 2:2
I know thy works, and thy labour, and thy patience, and how thou canst not bear them which are evil: and thou hast tried them which say they are apostles, and are not, and hast found them liars:
Matt 24:12
And because iniquity shall abound, the love of many shall wax cold.
corruption_summary: First love faces no postmodern redefinition; the principle to recover is the warning that sound doctrine and labor cannot replace warm love to Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The Ephesian danger is the peculiar peril of the orthodox: that a church zealous for truth, diligent in works, and discerning of error may yet let its love to Christ grow cold. The very strengths Christ commends — labor, patience, doctrinal vigilance — can mask a cooling heart, for they continue by habit and conviction even as affection wanes. "The love of many shall wax cold" (Matt 24:12) is fulfilled not only in apostates but in the dutiful.

The principle to recover is that Christ wants the heart, not merely the hands. He will not be content with a sound creed and a busy calendar if the warmth of love is gone. The remedy is not less doctrine or less labor, but love restored to govern both: "remember... and repent, and do the first works" (Rev 2:5). This dictionary confesses that the chief commandment is to love the Lord with all the heart (Matt 22:37), and that the cure for a cooled church is to return, in remembrance and repentance, to the deeds that flowed from its first love.
roots_summary: The phrase recalls the new convert's earliest and warmest devotion to Christ, which the Ephesians had let cool though their works continued.
roots_lines: First, the earliest, the devotion of the beginning.
Love here is ardent affection toward Christ Himself.
Ephesus kept the works but left the warmth that bore them.
Christ counts the cooling a fall to be repented of.
The first works flow again from love restored.
usage: A church may keep sound doctrine and yet leave its first love.
Christ's remedy for lost first love is to remember, repent, and do the first works.
First love is recovered not by more labor but by warmed affection to Christ.

etymology: Latin loci communes, "common places," the headings or topics under which a subject is ordered; the title of Philip Melanchthon's systematic theology of 1521.
biblical_def: The Loci Communes is Philip Melanchthon's 1521 work, reckoned the first systematic theology of the Protestant Reformation. Its title means "common places" — the standard topics, or loci, under which doctrine is gathered and treated in order: sin, law, grace, justification, faith, and the rest. This dictionary honors its landmark service. Drawing on Luther's rediscovery of the gospel and following the order of Paul's epistle to the Romans, Melanchthon set out the doctrines of grace with a clarity that schooled a generation, exalting justification by faith alone and the bondage of the fallen will to sin. Luther himself praised the book extravagantly. Yet faithfulness requires this dictionary to name where Melanchthon later erred. In his maturing editions he drifted toward synergism — the teaching that the human will cooperates with grace in conversion, contributing its own assent so that the Spirit, the Word, and the will are made three concurring causes. This compromises the monergism of effectual calling, in which God alone gives the new birth and raises the dead in sin to life (Eph 2:1-5; John 1:13). The will does not assist its own regeneration; it is renewed by sovereign grace. This dictionary confesses the unconditional, monergistic work of God in salvation, and so honors the Loci as a Reformation landmark while marking its author's later synergistic drift as error.
webster_summary: Melanchthon's 1521 work, the first Protestant systematic theology, ordering doctrine by "common places." A Reformation landmark, marred by its author's later synergistic drift on the will.
webster_full: LOCI COMMUNES, noun. "Common places"; Philip Melanchthon's 1521 work, the first systematic theology of the Reformation.
Orders doctrine by topical headings following Paul's epistle to the Romans.
"Even when we were dead in sins, hath quickened us together with Christ" (Eph 2:5).
Exalted justification by faith alone and the bondage of the fallen will.
Its author later drifted into synergism, an error this dictionary names as such.
scriptures: Eph 2:5
Even when we were dead in sins, hath quickened us together with Christ, (by grace ye are saved;)
John 1:13
Which were born, not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God.
Rom 9:16
So then it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy.
Phil 2:13
For it is God which worketh in you both to will and to do of his good pleasure.
corruption_summary: The error is not in the term but in its author: Melanchthon's later synergistic drift, teaching the will's cooperation in conversion, against the monergism of sovereign grace.
corruption_paragraphs: The Loci Communes stands as a genuine treasure of the Reformation's first years, ordering the recovered gospel into teachable form and pressing justification by faith alone upon the conscience. In its earliest edition Melanchthon wrote of the bound will and the sovereignty of grace in terms his fellow Reformers could embrace. This dictionary honors the work and the gift of its author, who labored beside Luther to set the church back upon the Word.

The error to name is Melanchthon's later movement toward synergism. In revised editions he taught that conversion involves three concurring causes — the Spirit, the Word, and the assenting human will — granting the will a cooperating part in its own quickening. But Scripture leaves no such room: men are "dead in sins" and quickened by God (Eph 2:5), born "not of the will of man, but of God" (John 1:13); mercy is "not of him that willeth... but of God" (Rom 9:16). To make the will a co-cause is to deny the monergism of effectual calling. This dictionary honors the landmark and names the drift, confessing that salvation is wholly of grace, for it is God who works in us both to will and to do (Phil 2:13).
roots_summary: The title means "common places," the topical headings under which doctrine is ordered; Melanchthon made it the title of the Reformation's first systematic theology.
roots_lines: Latin locus, a place; plural loci, places or topics.
Communes, common — the standard headings of a subject.
A locus communis was a recognized topic for ordered treatment.
Melanchthon gathered Christian doctrine under such headings in 1521.
The method shaped Protestant systematic theology thereafter.
usage: Melanchthon's Loci Communes gave the Reformation its first ordered theology.
Luther praised the Loci Communes as worthy to stand beside Scripture in usefulness.
Later editions of the Loci Communes reveal Melanchthon's drift toward synergism.
